intro_cards.title: About these notes
body: 8 units · tectonics to contours

Grade 12 is “geography of Eritrea in depth”. Grade 11 is the toolkit: how the crust moves, how water and wind carve, how people settle, then a first look at Eritrea’s place, relief and contour maps. Read each unit as a *story with a cause* — examiners mark the cause, not only the landform name.

intro_cards.title: Worked contour gradient
body: Two points: 1 200 m and 1 000 m. Map distance between them is 4 cm. Scale 1:50 000 (1 cm = 500 m).
Rise = 200 m. Run = 4 × 500 = 2 000 m. Gradient = 200/2000 = 1 in 10 (or 10%). Write both the fraction and a sentence: “For every 10 m walked horizontally you climb 1 m.”

f2.title: Tap-level sketch (same idea as Grade 12). East drainage to the Red Sea; west to Sudan; some streams die in Danakil.

cards.title: Relief — five belts to be able to sketch
body:
1. **Western lowlands** — broad, hot, falling toward Sudan. Sorghum / pastoral country; rivers like Barka and Gash.
2. **Highlands** — the spine. Cooler, more densely settled, rain-fed cereals. Asmara sits here.
3. **Eastern escarpment** — a steep drop toward the sea. Orographic moisture can make this the greenest strip; roads zigzag.
4. **Coastal plain** — narrow, hot, humid to arid depending on stretch; Massawa and the ports.
5. **Danakil / southern depression** — below or near sea level in parts, extreme heat, salt, rift geology (tie back to Unit 1).

cards.title: Classify Eritrea's relief regions
cards.problem: Name the three relief divisions of Eritrea and give the altitude, one feature and one economic use of each.

steps.text: **Step 1: Lowlands (below about 1,500 m).** Eastern lowlands (coastal plains, average 60 km wide, mostly below 500 m, include the Danakil Depression): salt, fishing, geothermal energy, tourism. Western lowlands (500–1,000 m, Barka, Gash and Setit): large-scale irrigated farming.
**Step 2: Eastern escarpment.** Tectonic in origin, cut by deep valleys (Haddas, Comayli); wet green Bahri slopes: tourism, irrigation in valley bottoms; steep slopes make roads costly.
**Step 3: Highlands.** Central plateau above about 1,500 m, highest point Emba Soira (3,013 m): cool climate, farming and dense population.

cards.answer: Lowlands (eastern and western), eastern escarpment and highlands, each with the altitude, features and uses described in the steps.

**Step 2:** It is one of the hottest places on earth, with lava fields and hot springs.

cards.title: Tap-level sketch (same idea as Grade 12). East drainage to the Red Sea; west to Sudan; some streams die in Danakil.
Drainage — three stories, not one national river
body: **Eastern system:** short, steep catchments racing down the escarpment to the Red Sea. Flashy after rain; little room for long flood plains.
**Western system:** longer rivers (Barka, Anseba, Gash–Mereb, Setit on the border) that drain toward Sudan. More useful for alluvial farming where the bed is wide, still seasonal.
**Danakil interior:** some streams never reach the sea; they evaporate or sink in the depression. Endorheic = closed basin.
Lakes in Eritrea are few and often seasonal or coastal / lagoonal rather than great inland seas. Do not invent a “Lake Victoria of Eritrea” on the paper.

cards.title: 7.3 Lakes in Eritrea
body: In Eritrea, there are no significant natural lakes.
Lake Bordole is located in the Buri Peninsula where salt is extracted.
Lake Bada and Lake Aba Adad are found in the Danakil Depression.
All are salty lakes, which carry water during the rainy season and dry up during the dry season.
Depositions are found in the lower sections of the river courses.

cards.title: Seasonal salt lakes and the character of Eritrea's rivers
body: Eritrea has **no large permanent natural lakes**. The lakes that exist are **seasonal and salty**: **Lake Bordole** on the Buri Peninsula (where salt is extracted) and **Lake Bada** and **Lake Aba Adad** in the Danakil Depression. They fill in the rainy season and dry up in the dry season, leaving salt crusts.

Main characteristics of Eritrea's rivers: (a) the major rivers rise in the wet highlands; (b) they are seasonal, except the **Setit**; (c) many follow straight courses controlled by faults; (d) they have strong erosive power because of steep slopes, and deposit material in their lower courses; (e) most fail to reach the sea and sink into the sand.

The only natural lakes are in the Eastern Lowlands south of the Gulf of Zula. Most stored water comes from **man-made dams and reservoirs** (for example Mai Nefhi and Gerset), which are vital for towns and irrigation.

cards.title: Explain why Eritrea's lakes are seasonal and salty
cards.problem: Explain why the lakes of the Danakil, such as Lake Bada, contain water only part of the year and are salty.

steps.text: **Step 1: Water supply.** They receive water only from seasonal rains and floods running off the escarpment.
**Step 2: Water loss.** The Danakil is one of the hottest places on Earth, so evaporation is very high.
**Step 3: Seasonal pattern.** In the dry season evaporation exceeds inflow and the lakes dry up.
**Step 4: Salt.** The lakes have no outlet; dissolved salts brought in by the water stay behind when it evaporates, so salt accumulates.
**Conclusion:** seasonal inflow, very high evaporation and no outlet make them seasonal salt lakes.

cards.answer: They are fed only by seasonal rain and floods, lose water by intense evaporation, and have no outlet, so they dry up in the dry season and leave salt behind.

cards.why:
**Step 1:** Lake Bordole is on the Buri Peninsula and salt is extracted there.

**Step 2:** Lake Bada and Lake Aba Adad are in the Danakil Depression.

**Step 3:** Lake Tana is in Ethiopia.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which is a characteristic of most Eritrean rivers?

options.A: They are seasonal and many sink into the sand before reaching the sea.
options.B: They rise in the coastal lowlands.

cards.why:
**Step 1:** Most rivers flow only in the rainy season (the Setit is the exception).

**Step 2:** Many lose their water into sandy plains before reaching the sea.

**Step 3:** They rise in the highlands and have steep slopes.

**Tip:** Read every option against the rule before choosing.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Lakes in the Danakil Depression are salty mainly because ____.

options.A: water evaporates quickly and the dissolved salts are left behind
options.B: sea water flows into them every day

cards.why:
**Step 1:** Inflowing water carries dissolved salts.

**Step 2:** Intense heat evaporates the water, but the salts remain.

**Step 3:** With no outlet, salt accumulates over time.

tips.text: The present relief of Eritrea is highly diversified and consists of different types of features that include mountain ranges, deep gorges, plains and offshore islands.
The country’s relief is broadly divided into three major divisions. These are the Highlands, the Lowlands and the Escarpments.
The Highlands extend from south to north.
The Northern Highlands are very much dissected by major river systems such as River Anseba.
The Central Plateau occupies geographically important location as major rivers of Eritrea originate from this plateau.

The Southern Plateau is agriculturally rich because of its flat terrain, adequate rainfall and fertile soil. There are two major divisions of lowlands. These are the Eastern Lowlands and the Western Lowlands.
Eritrea has a drainage system, which is divided into three major groups: The Eastern Drainage System, Western Drainage System and rivers that drain into the Danakil Depression.
Most of the rivers are seasonal in character with high erosive power due to the steep slopes.

questions.q: Which of the following rivers **does not** flow towards the Red Sea?
why: The **Anseba River** flows northwards and is a major tributary of the Barka River. The Barka-Anseba system flows towards the plains of Sudan (Western Drainage). Rivers like Alighede, Hadas, Felket, and Labka flow eastward into the Red Sea (Eastern Drainage).
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.

questions.q: One of the following rivers **does not** drain towards the east.
why: The Mereb River (known as the Gash in its lower course) flows westward toward the Sudanese plains. Rivers like Felket, Labka, Haddas, and Comayle all drain eastward into the Red Sea.
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.

questions.q: Which one of the following Eritrean Rivers enter to the Red sea through **Marsa Teklay**?

questions.q: Which of the following major rivers in Eritrea originates from west of Asmara around Adi Guadad and Mai Nefhi and flows toward western lowland?
why: River Barka originates in the central highlands of Eritrea, specifically in the areas west of Asmara near Adi Guadad. It flows in a northwesterly direction through the western lowlands toward the Sudanese border.
